issues.legal_issue: A statutory power to resume transferred property and forfeit payments for default is discriminatory when the authority may choose among recovery methods without statutory guidance and the forfeiture route offers no relief against forfeiture.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired a site at public auction, paid part of the purchase price, and defaulted on the remaining instalments.
The governing scheme secured unpaid consideration by a charge on the property and also allowed recovery through a public-revenue process.
The scheme separately allowed resumption of the site and forfeiture of payments, without guidance on when the authority should choose that route rather than another recovery method.
Ordinary law provided relief against forfeiture, but the statutory forfeiture route did not.
issues.conclusion: The statutory power to resume the site and forfeit payments violated Article 14 because it allowed unguided and discriminatory choices among recovery methods.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits arbitrary and discriminatory statutory powers. Under Sections 3, 8 and 9 of the Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952, unpaid consideration was secured by a charge, the amount due could be recovered through the statutory revenue-recovery procedure, and the authority could also resume the property and forfeit payments. The Court held that the lack of guidance for choosing among these remedies, together with the absence of relief against statutory forfeiture that was available under ordinary law, made the power discriminatory. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.unpaid_consideration_secured_by_charge: The governing arrangement secured unpaid purchase consideration by a charge over the transferred property.
predicates.alternative_recovery_routes_available: The authority could pursue more than one route to recover unpaid consideration.
predicates.no_selection_guidance: The governing law gave the authority no criteria for choosing among the recovery routes.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a property-recovery scheme that secures unpaid consideration but offers unguided recovery alternatives and forfeiture without ordinary relief, the resumption and forfeiture power is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: Resuming transferred property and forfeiting payments for unpaid consideration imposes an unreasonable restriction on the enjoyment of property when the unpaid amount is secured by an enforceable charge.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired the site at public auction, paid part of the price, and defaulted on the remaining instalments.

The governing scheme created a charge over the property for unpaid consideration and restricted the purchaser from transferring an interest in the property before the charge was paid, except with permission.
Despite that security, the authority resumed the site and forfeited the payments already made.
issues.conclusion: Resumption of the site and forfeiture of payments for the default imposed an unreasonable restriction on the enjoyment of property and violated Article 19(1)(f).
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) protects the right to property. The Court considered Sections 3 and 9 of the Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952, and the ordinary enforcement of a property charge under the Transfer of Property Act. Because the unpaid amount was secured by a charge that could be enforced through a suit and sale, the Court held it unreasonable to allow resumption and forfeiture for non-payment. No earlier cases are cited.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser in a completed sale owns the transferred property subject to a charge for unpaid consideration, rather than leaving the seller as owner until the entire price is paid.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired the site at a public auction and paid part of the purchase price, leaving instalments unpaid.
The governing scheme treated the unpaid consideration as a charge on the site and restricted further transfer of the purchaser’s interest until the charge was paid, except with permission.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser held ownership rights in the site, subject to the charge for the unpaid consideration; the seller did not remain the owner merely because the full price had not been paid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952, provided for sale to a transferee, made unpaid consideration a first charge on the property, and restricted the transferee’s ability to sell, mortgage or otherwise transfer an interest before payment of the charge. The Court held that those provisions recognized the transferee’s ownership rights and were inconsistent with the seller remaining owner until full payment. No earlier cases are cited.

issues.definition: When a completed sale gives the purchaser a recognized property interest and secures the unpaid balance by a charge, the purchaser owns the property subject to that charge.
